pos.personaBrief: Chapman's side was built around counter-attacking speed, with Buchan's aim of goals from three or four touches out of defence and transitions the club history stresses, so possession is a means rather than the goal. Sources describe quick incisive passing and midfield dominance, but not a possession obsession.

pro.personaBrief: Buchan's counter-attacking aim of a goal from three or four touches out of defence and the transitions cited by Arsenal.com point to direct, fast progression once the ball is won. Short build-up under pressure and sideways passing are not documented as features of this side.

est.personaBrief: The WM shape (3-2-2-3 / 3-4-3) gives each player a fixed role and position, as described by Wikipedia and These Football Times. The roving inside-forward (Andy Neil) and the fixed penetrating forward show a structure of defined zones rather than a rondo-style relational play.

lar.personaBrief: This axis has no verified evidence, so this comes from general knowledge: Chapman's Arsenal relied on wingers such as Joe Hulme and Cliff Bastin to stretch the pitch and deliver from the flanks, and the WM shape kept two wide attackers. Central play was used, but width was a core weapon.

blo.personaBrief: The Scots Football Historians' Group describes a defensive-distributive model, and the offside change let the side keep two defenders behind the ball, which favours a compact, deep block that waits in its own half. No verified source describes pressing the build-up, so the team is answered as reactive rather than high-pressing.

mar.personaBrief: Woolwich Arsenal credits Charlie Buchan with zonal marking for one player, and the SFHG describes wing-halves marking the wingers, so the marking method is contested. Zonal protection of spaces is the closest documented approach, with a genuine split on the man-marking question.

pla.personaBrief: Chapman arrived with his own system and reshaped the club around it, and the 1925 tactical change was driven by his own plan. He adjusted after the 7-0 defeat, but the core identity stayed the same, so the own-way answers lean towards identity over adaptation.

res.personaBrief: Arsenal under Chapman won the 1930-31, 1932-33 and 1933-34 titles, and the club history stresses that fans and results mattered, while the counter-attacking football was also praised as spectacle. The results-first answers are strongest, with a tilt toward valuing attractive football.

sis.personaBrief: Chapman's system was the centre of the team, with defined roles like the WM shape and the boot room running the system, and the Arsenal.com feature says he was a master tactician. Talent mattered, but it was placed inside a collective structure that every player had to serve.

jog.personaBrief: This axis has no verified evidence, so this comes from general knowledge: Chapman's side leaned on technical inside-forwards such as Alex James and on a classic playmaking inside-forward, while physical strength was less central. Technique was valued above athleticism.

bas.personaBrief: Chapman championed nursery and feeder teams, which the Arsenal.com feature records, so developing players counted for a lot. But he also bought established players and experienced figures to win titles, so the squad was not built only from the academy.

lid.personaBrief: Chapman is described as a disciplinarian who was also hugely supportive of his players, and he entrusted a select group of men through the boot room. He kept clear authority and the rules, while consulting trusted senior figures.
